the most vital, and prokinetics and antiemetics are the pri-
mary medical therapies (see Table 27-3). Metoclopramide and 
erythromycin are medications that may be used to promote 
gastric motility. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, appe-
tite, ileal brake (the slowing effect of intestinal transit of 
undigested food, often fat, reaching the ileum), or formation 
of a bezoar (concentration of undigested material in the 
stomach) are other factors that may affect nutritional status. 
In a select patient population, implantation of gastric pace-
makers may be advantageous to improve gastric emptying 
(Ross et al, 2014).
Bezoar formation may be related to undigested food such as 
cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin and fruit tannins (phytobezoars), 
or medications (pharmacobezoars) such as cholestyramine, 
sucralfate, enteric-coated aspirin, aluminum-containing antac-
ids, and bulk-forming laxatives. Treatment of bezoars includes 
enzyme therapy (such as papain, bromelain, or cellulase), lavage, 
and sometimes endoscopic therapy to mechanically break up the 
bezoar. Most patients respond to some combination of medica-
tion and dietary intervention; however, unresponsive and more
